verification.spec: Since CWM-on-Twine is a Meta-internal endpoint not reproducible externally, verify structurally: import the CWM backend class, confirm it implements the LLMBackend interface, and inspect its generate() method to confirm it issues HTTP/RPC requests to a configurable Twine endpoint URL (e.g., via env var TWINE_CWM_ENDPOINT) and adapts the response into the backend interface. Mock the endpoint with a local HTTP server returning a canned response and verify end-to-end.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that integrates the Llama model as an internal LLM backend served on Twine, using the same backend interface as CWM so backends are interchangeable in the search loop.

verification.spec: Import the Llama backend class and verify it implements the same LLMBackend interface as CWM (same abstract methods, same signatures). Mock the Twine Llama endpoint with a local HTTP server returning a canned kernel-shaped response and verify end-to-end that backend.generate() returns the mocked text. Confirm the search loop can swap between Llama and CWM by changing only the backend name.

sub_tasks.requirements: The dynamic prompt synthesizer composes context-augmented prompts that are consumed by every backend through the universal operator.

Code has been implemented for a dynamic prompt synthesizer that assembles per-iteration prompts from (a) the current kernel implementation and execution history, (b) LLM-generated analysis reports from the context memory sub-agent, (c) retrieved knowledge-base content from the deep search sub-agent, and (d) hardware-specific constraints, replacing static per-operator prompt templates.

verification.spec: Construct a fake iteration state containing (a) a current kernel source, (b) a context-memory analysis report string, (c) retrieved knowledge-base snippets, and pass to the PromptSynthesizer. Verify the returned prompt string contains substrings from all three inputs (indicating all sections were assembled) and that removing any input reduces the prompt correspondingly.

sub_tasks.requirements: The prompt synthesizer enforces a configurable token budget per backend (e.g., 64K-1M tokens depending on LLM) by prioritizing context sections based on profiling evidence and truncating or deferring lower-priority content, and this budget is set per-backend rather than hardcoded globally.

verification.spec: Construct a PromptSynthesizer with per-backend token budgets (e.g., claude=200000, gpt=128000, cwm=64000) supplied via config, not hardcoded. Feed it an oversized context with many low-priority sections; verify (a) synthesized prompt token count (measured with tiktoken or backend tokenizer) is <= configured budget, (b) high-priority sections tied to profiling evidence appear while lower-priority ones are truncated, (c) changing budget config changes the truncation boundary.

sub_tasks.requirements: The universal operator invokes exactly one LLM backend call per search-graph expansion using the synthesized prompt (rather than issuing separate calls per Draft/Debug/Improve operator), and the returned text is parsed into a candidate kernel artifact for downstream evaluation.

verification.spec: Mock the LLM backend to count generate() invocations. Trigger one expansion of the tree-search graph (universal operator applied to one parent node). Assert the backend was called exactly once. Verify the returned text is parsed (e.g., code block extraction) into a candidate kernel artifact stored in the object store with a valid path_ref.

sub_tasks.requirements: Backend integration is verified end-to-end on a smoke kernel-generation task.

verification.spec: Run a small end-to-end smoke test: configure a real LLM backend (e.g., Claude 4.5 or GPT-5 with API key), invoke KernelEvolve on a trivial kernel-generation task (e.g., elementwise ReLU in Triton with a PyTorch reference), and verify that at least one candidate is generated, evaluated, and stored with a fitness score > 0. Assert the smoke test completes in < 15 minutes.

sub_tasks.requirements: KernelEvolve achieves 100% pass rate on all 250 problems across three difficulty levels of the KernelBench suite, validating the framework's ability to generate correct GPU kernels for canonical operators, kernel fusion patterns, and full model implementations.
The KernelBench benchmark suite is acquired and its 250 problems are organized by the three difficulty levels defined in the original KernelBench paper.
Code has been implemented to download or clone the KernelBench dataset (Ouyang et al., 2025) containing the full 250 problems and their PyTorch reference implementations.

verification.spec: Run the dataset download/clone script and verify that the resulting local directory contains the KernelBench source tree with the three level subdirectories and 250 PyTorch reference .py files in total (matching the counts from Ouyang et al. 2025). Assert `git remote -v` (if cloned) points at the KernelBench repository.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that partitions the 250 KernelBench problems into the three difficulty levels (Level 1: single operators, Level 2: kernel fusion, Level 3: full model) as defined by the benchmark specification.

verification.spec: Call the partitioning function and inspect the returned mapping {'level1': [...], 'level2': [...], 'level3': [...]}. Verify each list contains problem IDs consistent with the KernelBench benchmark spec (Level 1 = single operators, Level 2 = fusion, Level 3 = full model architectures) and that lists are disjoint.

sub_tasks.requirements: The count of problems retrieved and enumerated for evaluation across all three levels sums to exactly 250, matching the full KernelBench suite.

verification.spec: After enumerating problems across all three levels, assert len(level1) + len(level2) + len(level3) == 250. Also assert there are no duplicate problem IDs across levels.

sub_tasks.requirements: The KernelBench evaluation harness invokes KernelEvolve on each problem and measures pass/fail against the reference PyTorch implementation.
Code has been implemented that, for each KernelBench problem, extracts the PyTorch reference module and input-generator so KernelEvolve receives a well-defined kernel specification as input.

verification.spec: For a sampled KernelBench problem, call the extraction utility and verify it returns (a) a callable PyTorch nn.Module or reference function, and (b) an input-generator (callable) that, when invoked, produces torch.Tensor inputs of shapes consistent with the KernelBench spec. Run the reference module on generated inputs to confirm it executes without error.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that drives the KernelEvolve tree-search loop per problem until either a correct Triton kernel is produced or the termination rule (budget/time) is reached, and records the final generated kernel artifact.

verification.spec: Run KernelEvolve on 2-3 sampled KernelBench problems with a small budget (e.g., max 5 iterations or 10 minutes each). Verify (a) the loop terminates in all cases, (b) the final artifact per problem is written to the object store, (c) a termination reason is recorded ('correct', 'budget_exhausted', or 'time_exhausted').

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to compile and execute each generated Triton kernel on the target hardware backend and capture its outputs alongside the PyTorch reference outputs.

verification.spec: For a sample generated Triton kernel, invoke the compile+execute utility on the target backend, then run the paired PyTorch reference. Verify both return torch.Tensor outputs of matching dtype and shape, and both are captured (returned as a tuple or stored under a comparison record) for downstream torch.allclose checking.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that classifies a KernelBench problem as PASSED only if the generated Triton kernel compiles, runs without errors, and satisfies torch.allclose numerical equivalence against the PyTorch reference across all specified input shapes.

verification.spec: Feed the classifier three fixtures: (1) a correct Triton kernel that torch.allclose matches PyTorch across all input shapes -> expect PASSED, (2) a kernel that raises at compile time -> expect FAILED, (3) a kernel that runs but produces outputs off by 1e-1 (exceeding torch.allclose default tolerances) -> expect FAILED. Verify the classifier decisions match.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that persists per-problem pass/fail status, generated kernel source, and any error diagnostics to enable auditing of the 250-problem sweep.

verification.spec: After running a small sweep over N=3 problems, verify persisted records exist per problem: pass/fail flag in metadata store, generated kernel .py file in object store, and any error string / stack trace field populated for failing runs. Query the metadata store and confirm all N problem IDs are present with the expected schema.

sub_tasks.requirements: Per-level and aggregate pass-rate numbers are computed and match the paper's headline KernelBench claim.
Code has been implemented that aggregates the per-problem pass/fail results and reports pass rate separately for Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 of KernelBench.

verification.spec: Run the aggregation function over a mock metadata store populated with per-problem results tagged by level. Verify it emits pass_rate_level1, pass_rate_level2, pass_rate_level3 as floats in [0,1], each computed as passes/total for that level. Verify with hand-constructed inputs that the arithmetic matches expectations.

sub_tasks.requirements: KernelEvolve achieves 100% pass rate on Level 1 (single operator) problems of KernelBench.

verification.spec: Execute KernelEvolve end-to-end over all Level-1 KernelBench problems on an H100, using the paper's configuration (universal operator, tree search, at least one supported LLM backend, sufficient per-problem budget). Compute pass_rate_level1 = (# problems whose final kernel is classified PASSED by the torch.allclose evaluator) / (# level-1 problems). Report pass_rate_level1 as a fraction in [0,1].

sub_tasks.requirements: KernelEvolve achieves 100% pass rate on Level 2 (kernel fusion) problems of KernelBench.

verification.spec: Run KernelEvolve over all Level 2 (kernel fusion) problems of KernelBench and compute pass rate = correct/total. Expect 100%.

sub_tasks.requirements: KernelEvolve achieves 100% pass rate on Level 3 (full model) problems of KernelBench.

verification.spec: Run KernelEvolve over all Level 3 (full model) problems of KernelBench and compute pass rate. Expect 100%.

sub_tasks.requirements: The aggregate pass rate across all 250 KernelBench problems (Level 1 + Level 2 + Level 3) is 100%, matching the abstract's reported result.

verification.spec: Aggregate KernelEvolve results across all 250 KernelBench problems (Levels 1+2+3) and compute overall pass rate. Expect 250/250 = 100%.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to emit a final summary table or report enumerating, for each of the 250 problems, its level, its pass/fail status, and the total count of passes = 250.

verification.spec: Invoke the reporting entry point after a KernelBench run; assert output contains rows for 250 problems each with level in {1,2,3} and pass/fail status, and prints total passes==250.

sub_tasks.requirements: KernelEvolve achieves 100% correctness across 480 operator-platform configurations covering 160 PyTorch ATen operators on three heterogeneous hardware platforms (NVIDIA, AMD, MTIA).
The evaluation suite covers 160 PyTorch ATen operators drawn from the OSS operator space, matching the scope reported in Section 4.
Code has been implemented that enumerates a fixed, reproducible list of exactly 160 PyTorch ATen operators used as the OSS operator evaluation benchmark.

verification.spec: Import the operator suite module and assert it exposes a static list/enumeration of 160 ATen operator identifiers used for the OSS evaluation.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented so that loading the operator suite yields exactly 160 distinct ATen operator identifiers with no duplicates and each entry resolvable to a callable PyTorch reference.

verification.spec: Load the operator suite, assert len(set(ops))==160, and for each op verify it resolves to a callable PyTorch reference (getattr on torch.ops.aten or documented equivalent).

sub_tasks.requirements: The number of ATen operators reported in the OSS operator evaluation equals 160 as claimed in the Abstract and Section 4.

verification.spec: Count the number of ATen operators reported in the OSS operator evaluation results table; expect exactly 160.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that verifies every operator in the suite corresponds to a valid PyTorch ATen operator (present in torch.ops.aten or its documented equivalent).

verification.spec: For each operator id in the suite, assert it resolves via torch.ops.aten (or documented equivalent) to an existing callable; raise on invalid entries.

sub_tasks.requirements: The evaluation runs each of the 160 operators on three heterogeneous hardware platforms (NVIDIA GPU, AMD GPU, MTIA), producing 3 platform configurations per operator.
Code has been implemented that registers the three target platforms (NVIDIA, AMD, MTIA) as evaluation targets and dispatches operator runs to the appropriate hardware interpreter for each.

verification.spec: Import the platform-dispatch module and assert it registers exactly the three targets {NVIDIA, AMD, MTIA}, each with a dispatch function pointing to the respective hardware interpreter.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that constructs the 160 x 3 = 480 (operator, platform) configuration matrix and iterates over every pair for evaluation.

verification.spec: Call the configuration-enumeration function and assert it yields exactly 480 unique (operator, platform) pairs covering the full 160x3 matrix.

sub_tasks.requirements: The total number of operator-platform configurations evaluated in the OSS operator study equals 480.

verification.spec: After evaluation, count rows in the results table for OSS operator study; expect exactly 480 (operator, platform) configurations.

sub_tasks.requirements: For every (operator, platform) configuration, KernelEvolve invokes its end-to-end generation pipeline to produce a Triton kernel candidate targeted at that platform.
Code has been implemented that launches the KernelEvolve tree-search kernel generation pipeline once per (operator, platform) configuration and stores the resulting best kernel artifact.

verification.spec: Run the pipeline over a small sample of configurations and assert that for each (operator, platform) a best-kernel artifact file is written to the object store with the expected metadata linkage.

sub_tasks.requirements: Each produced kernel artifact conforms to the dual PytorchModel / TritonModel nn.Module output format with matching forward signatures and a get_inputs() function.

verification.spec: Load a produced artifact file, import it, assert it exposes classes PytorchModel and TritonModel (both nn.Module subclasses) with matching forward signatures and a module-level get_inputs() callable returning a list of tensor tuples.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that persists each generated kernel and its metadata (operator id, platform, fitness, correctness flag) so that the 480 results can be aggregated for the correctness report.

verification.spec: After a run, query the metadata store and assert each entry contains operator id, platform, fitness score, and is_buggy flag, and that path_ref resolves to the persisted kernel file.

sub_tasks.requirements: Each generated Triton kernel is validated for numerical correctness against the PyTorch ATen reference on multiple input shapes per operator using torch.allclose with appropriate tolerances.
Code has been implemented that generates multiple input tensor shapes per operator (via each artifact's get_inputs()) covering diverse scales for correctness testing.

verification.spec: Call get_inputs() on several generated artifacts and assert it returns multiple input configurations spanning distinct tensor shapes/sizes used for correctness testing.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that compares Triton kernel outputs to PyTorch reference outputs using torch.allclose with precision-dependent tolerances and marks the configuration as correct only if all input sizes pass.

verification.spec: Invoke the correctness comparator on Triton vs PyTorch outputs; assert it uses torch.allclose with precision-appropriate rtol/atol per dtype and only reports pass when ALL input sizes pass.

sub_tasks.requirements: Any configuration whose kernel fails compilation, raises a runtime error, or produces numerically mismatched outputs is recorded with is_buggy=True and fitness score 0 in the results store.

verification.spec: Inject a kernel with a compile error and a kernel with numerical mismatch; assert both result in metadata rows with is_buggy=True and fitness score 0.

sub_tasks.requirements: Correctness results across all 480 configurations are aggregated into an overall correctness rate and per-platform breakdown reproducing the reported 100% correctness claim.
Code has been implemented that aggregates per-configuration correctness outcomes across all 480 (operator, platform) pairs and computes an overall correctness percentage.

verification.spec: Run the aggregation function on the 480-row results and assert it produces overall_correct/480 as a percentage, matching the expected 100%.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that reports correctness counts separately for each of the three platforms (NVIDIA, AMD, MTIA), each covering all 160 operators.

verification.spec: Assert the aggregation output includes per-platform correctness counts for NVIDIA, AMD, and MTIA, each with denominator 160.

sub_tasks.requirements: The overall correctness rate across the 480 operator-platform configurations in the OSS operator evaluation equals 100% (480/480 configurations pass).

verification.spec: Compute (# correct configurations) / 480 * 100 over the OSS operator evaluation; expect 100%.

sub_tasks.requirements: Each of the three platforms individually achieves 160/160 correct operator configurations in the OSS operator evaluation.

verification.spec: For each platform in {NVIDIA, AMD, MTIA}, count correct operator configurations; expect 160/160 for each.

sub_tasks.requirements: The OSS operator evaluation is reproducible via deterministic drivers, fixed seeds, and documented budgets so the 100%/480 result can be re-derived.
Code has been implemented that seeds all random input generation used in the OSS operator correctness evaluation so results are deterministic across runs.

verification.spec: Run get_inputs() twice under the same seed configuration and assert identical tensor values (bitwise equal), confirming random input generation is seeded and deterministic.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that exposes and records the tree-search budget (maximum iterations or wall-clock) used per configuration in the OSS operator evaluation.

verification.spec: Inspect the run configuration/results and assert that per-configuration tree-search budget (max iterations or wall-clock) is recorded and accessible in the metadata.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that exports the full 480-row results table (operator, platform, correctness, fitness) for inspection and audit.

verification.spec: Invoke the export function and assert it produces a table (CSV/JSON) with exactly 480 rows containing operator, platform, correctness, and fitness columns.

sub_tasks.requirements: The conv1d (6.5x) and conv2d (4.7x) speedups reported for convolutional transformer workloads are reproduced, including workload setup, kernel generation, correctness validation, and performance measurement.

The convolutional transformer workloads (conv1d and conv2d) are correctly set up as PyTorch reference implementations with the input shapes and configurations described in Section 5.1/5.2 and Appendix A.
Code has been implemented that defines a PyTorch reference `nn.Module` for the 1D convolution workload (Appendix A) used as the baseline for measuring conv1d speedup.

verification.spec: Import the conv1d workload module and assert it defines a PytorchModel(nn.Module) implementing the 1D convolution baseline described in Appendix A, with expected constructor and forward signature.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that defines a PyTorch reference `nn.Module` for the 2D convolution workload used as the baseline for measuring conv2d speedup.

verification.spec: Import the module containing the conv2d PyTorch reference. Assert that a class named `PytorchModel` (or equivalent baseline module) exists, is an `nn.Module` subclass, and instantiates successfully. Assert its `forward` method runs a 2D convolution on a sample input tensor and returns a tensor of the expected shape.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that generates conv1d and conv2d input tensors with the batch sizes, channel counts, spatial dimensions, kernel sizes, strides, and padding matching the convolutional transformer configuration described in Section 5.1 and Appendix A.

verification.spec: Call `get_inputs()` from the conv1d and conv2d modules. Assert the returned tensors have shapes consistent with the convolutional transformer configuration described in Section 5.1 and Appendix A (batch size, channel count, spatial dims, kernel size, stride, padding). Verify dtype is float32 and tensors are on the expected device.

sub_tasks.requirements: The `get_inputs()` function returns multiple input sizes so that speedup is measured across several problem scales as required by the KernelEvolve dual-implementation interface.

verification.spec: Call `get_inputs()` and assert it returns multiple distinct input configurations (list/tuple of length >= 2) with varying problem scales (e.g., different batch sizes or spatial dims), consistent with the KernelEvolve dual-implementation benchmarking interface.

sub_tasks.requirements: Optimized Triton kernels are generated for conv1d and conv2d following the KernelEvolve dual-implementation format (PyTorch baseline + Triton `nn.Module` with `@triton.jit` kernel).
